subject: Ingestion-rate SLO priming — post-call recap and runbook next steps
messages:
From: Diego Fernandez <diego_fernandez@redwood.com>
To: Taylor Ng <taylor@streamlytics.io>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-10-07T14:02:00-07:00
Subject: Ingestion-rate SLO priming — post-call recap and runbook next steps

Hi Taylor —

Thanks again for today's discussion. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we all have the same checklist before the tech deep-dive:

Recap (what we heard)
- Primary SLO: p95 end-to-end latency for streaming ingestion and response under normal load: target <= 250ms.
- Traffic profile: steady ingestion at ~700 qps with planned daily spikes to ~1,200 qps during batch windows.
- Concurrency pattern: many short-lived streaming sessions (~60–90s average), ~400 concurrent sessions normally, up to ~1,000 during peak.
- Streaming requirement: clients need server-side streaming with token flushes within 100–150ms; partial results acceptable.
- Constraint: Streamlytics must not see >1s p99 for production queries; some queueing acceptable for brief ramp events.

Proposed Redwood commitments to test in our readiness validation
1) Scale-up time: 99% of required capacity available within 90 seconds of a step ramp to 1,200 qps.
2) Warm-pool priming: maintain a configurable warm-pool equivalent to ~25% of peak concurrency (250 sessions) and demonstrate cold-start vs warm-start latency delta < 80ms for first token.
3) Queueing behavior: under emergencies, allow queueing with backpressure and graceful 503 fallback; queue latency should not push p95 beyond 500ms.
4) Streaming flushes: ensure token flush latency <150ms at p95 during peak.

Attachments: I attached the quick sample of the latency metrics you sent (latency-metrics-sample.csv) and our initial runbook proposal (redwood-runbook-proposal-v1.pdf).

Next steps (ask)
- Can you confirm the peak qps number is 1,200 (not accounting for short bursts >1,200)? Reply with any corrections.
- We propose a 45-minute technical deep-dive on Tue 2026-10-13 to walk the Redwood test plan and run the initial synthetic priming test. Please send an attendee list for SRE/infra folks.
- Marissa (cc'd): please prepare a short validation script that exercises the streaming flush path and emits token latency histograms.

Thanks — I’ll hold on scheduling until Taylor confirms availability.

Best,

Diego Fernandez
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
diego_fernandez@redwood.com | +1 (415) 555-0114

[Attachment: latency-metrics-sample.csv (CSV, 18KB)]
[Attachment: redwood-runbook-proposal-v1.pdf (PDF, 240KB)]

From: Taylor Ng <taylor@streamlytics.io>

Cc: Chris Li <chris@streamlytics.io>, ops@streamlytics.io
Date: 2026-10-07T17:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Ingestion-rate SLO priming — post-call recap and runbook next steps

Diego —

Thanks for the clear recap. A few clarifications from our side:
- Peak number: yes, 1,200 qps is the expected daily peak for the ingestion API. We do run micro-bursts up to ~1,500 qps for 10–30s, but those are exceptional and handled by client-side throttles if needed.
- Concurrency: your concurrency numbers look right — ~400 steady, up to ~1,000 regular peaks, 1,500 for extreme bursts.
- Streaming flush: target consumer experience is to see partial results within ~150ms, so your flush target aligns.

For the deep-dive on Tue 2026-10-13, tentative attendees from Streamlytics: Chris Li (SRE lead), Priya Anand (Product), and Sam Ortiz (infra). We can make it 45 mins starting 09:00 PT.

Also: two asks before the call
1) Can Redwood provide a simple synthetic generator we can run in our staging to reproduce the concurrency/profile?
2) Can you outline what instrumentation you will produce (prometheus metrics, per-token histograms, KV-cache hit metrics)?

We’re comfortable with the proposed runbook approach — Chris will review the PDF and comment inline.

—Taylor
Taylor Ng
Head of Platform Engineering | Streamlytics
taylor@streamlytics.io | +1 (206) 555-0199

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Taylor Ng <taylor@streamlytics.io>
Cc: Diego Fernandez <diego_fernandez@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-10-08T09:10:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Ingestion-rate SLO priming — post-call recap and runbook next steps

Hi Taylor —

Thanks — quick technical note before the deep-dive: Ben and I sketched an initial validation plan. High level:
- Synthetic generator: we’ll provide a containerized loadgen (Docker image + sample config) that reproduces session-based streaming with adjustable burst profiles. We’ll include a k6 script for HTTP streaming and a small Python client for token-level timing.
- Instrumentation: Redwood will supply Prometheus-compatible exporters for:
  * per-request latency (p50/p95/p99)
  * token-flush latency histograms
  * kv-cache hit rate
  * active concurrency gauge
  * queue length gauge when scaling events occur
- Acceptance criteria for the initial run:
  1) Under a controlled ramp to 1,200 qps (steady over 5m), p95 latency <= 250ms.
  2) Under a step-ramp (700 -> 1,200 qps within 60s), 99% capacity available within 90s, and p95 <= 350ms during ramp.
  3) Warm-pool priming test: pre-warm 250 sessions and measure first-token delta; target < 80ms.

We’ll attach the short k6 config and the command-line example to the Drive link prior to the call. Diego: Ben will own the loadgen and I’ll own the metrics collection + dashboards.

Ben — can you confirm we can produce the container image and the default configs by Friday 2026-10-09?

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Sr. Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com | +1 (650) 555-0222

Subject: Re: Ingestion-rate SLO priming — post-call recap and runbook next steps

Marissa, Diego —

Appreciate the detailed plan. Confirmed on the 09:00 PT slot for 2026-10-13; I’ll add the calendar invite and include our staging cluster access details.

Ben — if you can get the loadgen container by COB 2026-10-09 that gives our infra team time to stand up the test harness on Monday.

Couple of clarifying points from our infra checklist:
- During the step-ramp test, we want to see how Redwood handles backpressure when downstream services (our Kafka pipelines) have transient slowness. Please document the behavior and any circuit-breaker thresholds you enforce.
- For warm-pool sizing: can Redwood offer an autosize suggestion based on historical p99 start times from similar customers?

If those two items are in scope, we’re green to proceed.

Chris Li
